title: Gail Halvorsen, the Candy Bomber
text:
In June 1948 the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin, cutting road and rail links. The Western Allies answered with the Berlin Airlift, flying in food, coal and supplies around the clock. Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen was an American transport pilot flying into Tempelhof airport. Only three years earlier, Americans had been bombing the city.

One day in July 1948 he went to the airport fence and talked with a group of German children. He was struck that they asked for nothing. He had only two sticks of gum, and he broke them and passed them through the wire. The children shared the pieces and passed around the wrappers to smell them. Halvorsen promised to drop candy from his plane the next day. They asked how they would know his plane. He said he would wiggle his wings.

He and his crew tied candy to tiny parachutes made of handkerchiefs and dropped them on approach. Soon children waited daily for "Uncle Wiggly Wings." When his superiors found out, they made it an official operation, called Little Vittles, and American children and candy makers sent supplies. By the end of the airlift, crews had dropped tons of candy over Berlin.
lesson: A small kindness, especially to children, can change how a former enemy sees you. Notice the people at the fence, and give what you have.
source: Gail S. Halvorsen, The Berlin Candy Bomber (1990); US Air Force historical records of the Berlin Airlift
